organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Top leadership based in Afghanistan until Zawahiri's death; pledges allegiance to Hibatullah; uses Afghanistan for regrouping, training, fundraising, recruiting; no immediate external-ops capability per UN.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Hosts al-Qaeda leadership; 'Pashtun chauvinist movement'; fears defections to ISIL; described as '100% untrustworthy' by Fitton-Brown.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: 'Tactically autonomous part of the Taliban' with features of an intelligence organization; key al-Qaeda ally inside the de facto administration; looked after Zawahiri in Kabul and sanitised the strike site; holds key defense ministry positions.

organizations.name: AQIS
organizations.notes: 180-400 fighters, primarily from Bangladesh, India, Myanmar, Pakistan; represented at individual level among Taliban combat units; fought in 2021 takeover.

organizations.name: TTP
aliases: Movement of the Taliban in Pakistan
organizations.notes: 3,000-4,000 fighters inside Afghanistan; biggest foreign group; sworn enemy of the Pakistani state; close to Sirajuddin Haqqani; historic feeder to ISIL; al-Qaeda helped write its founding charter per bin Laden documents.

organizations.name: Turkestan Islamic Party
organizations.notes: Re-established main base in Baghlan province; elements moved west away from Badakhshan/China corridor; strengthening ties with TTP and Jamaat Ansarullah, IED training, planning attacks on Chinese interests 'when the time is right'; helped Taliban takeover.

organizations.name: Jamaat Ansarullah
organizations.notes: Tajik group 'in the al-Qaeda sphere'; controls five districts of Badakhshan under Mahdi Arsalan; Tajikistan believes the Taliban instrumentalise it against them.

organizations.name: Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Uzbek-linked group in Afghanistan; Uzbekistan 'fairly comfortable' with Taliban handling.

organizations.name: ISKP
organizations.notes: ~3,000-4,000 strong; failed rocket attacks on Tajik and Uzbek territory; attracts defectors from Taliban's Uzbek/Tajik/Uyghur ranks and ex-TTP.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: More immediate threat per member states; leadership Iraqi; propaganda now from remote provinces.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: 'Taliban of Africa'; constant cross-border threat to Kenya; emir Ahmed Diriye in al-Qaeda line of seniority; pilot-trainee plot in the Philippines.

organizations.name: AQAP
organizations.notes: Former aviation threat (bomb maker al-Asiri); inspired the Pensacola attack; weakened.

organizations.name: JNIM
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda coalition broadly under Mebrak; eroding governance in Mali, Burkina Faso, spreading to Senegal, Cote d'Ivoire, Togo, Benin, western Niger, possibly NW Nigeria.

organizations.name: Hurras al-Din
organizations.notes: Looked at external attacks but did not bring any off.

organizations.name: UN Security Council Monitoring Team
aliases: Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team

events.description: UN Monitoring Team report issued stating Zawahiri alive and communicating freely, al-Qaeda enjoys greater freedom in Afghanistan, and setting out the al-Qaeda line of seniority (Saif al-Adel, Maghrebi, Mebrak, Diriye).
US drone strike kills Ayman al-Zawahiri in a Kabul safe house purportedly run by Sirajuddin Haqqani / the Taliban interior ministry; Haqqani enablers later sanitised the site.
Zawahiri was reported dead in 2020; Roggio was skeptical; UN later confirmed him alive.
Taliban takeover of Afghanistan ('just under a year ago'); AQIS and Turkestan Islamic Party fighters took part; Zawahiri's communications became current and comfortable afterwards.
Roggio and Fitton-Brown met for breakfast in New York City and discussed whether the report implied Zawahiri was in Afghanistan.
Secretary Pompeo stated the Taliban would 'destroy al-Qaeda' as part of the US-Taliban deal.
Jamaat Ansarullah commander Mahdi Arsalan controls five districts of Badakhshan province (per UN report and Roggio's earlier 2022 reporting).
Turkestan Islamic Party re-established its main base in Baghlan province; elements moved westwards away from Badakhshan/China corridor.
US designation of Abdul Haq al-Turkistani identifying him as a member of al-Qaeda's executive council (Shura Majlis).
ISKP attempted rocket/missile strikes on Tajik and Uzbek territory that failed to achieve anything.
US military served as de facto 'air arm' for the Taliban against the Islamic State in Nangarhar (2016-2018) per Roggio.
TTP-Pakistan truce discussions; TTP demands described as extreme and unacceptable to Islamabad.
Death of Abu Muhammad al-Masri, after which the al-Qaeda 1-2-3 succession order (Zawahiri, Saif al-Adel, Maghrebi) was clear.

key_claims: Zawahiri's killing in a Haqqani-run Kabul safe house 'comprehensively disproves' Taliban denials that al-Qaeda is in Afghanistan.

The Haqqani Network is the key al-Qaeda ally inside the Taliban administration; Sirajuddin Haqqani is personally the most important single figure, more influential than Hibatullah or Yaqoob per Roggio.
Al-Qaeda pledges allegiance to Hibatullah; the relationship is a partnership not of equals, and the Taliban was never going to arrest, expel or hand over al-Qaeda.

Al-Qaeda uses Afghanistan for leadership basing, regrouping, training, fundraising and recruiting, and deliberately avoids external operations that would embarrass the Taliban; any attack would likely be outsourced to affiliates for deniability.
Saif al-Adel (in Iran) is the likely successor; Iran may keep him as leverage; his move to Afghanistan would be a key indicator.
The Taliban's 'protective hug or restraining hug' of >20 foreign terrorist groups (TTP, TIP/ETIM, Jamaat Ansarullah, IMU) is shaped by fear of defections to ISKP.
TTP is the biggest foreign group (3,000-4,000 in Afghanistan), close to Sirajuddin Haqqani, and the Taliban will not betray it to Pakistan.
Framing ISKP as the main threat leads to dangerous wishful thinking about counterterrorism cooperation with the Taliban.
